rv.q: Fear itself is something to fear in “The American Plan” by Richard Greenberg, an elegant and incisive 1990 play that has been given the revival it deserves by the Manhattan Theater Club. In David Grindley’s subtle yet shimmeringly clear production, which opened Thursday night at the Samuel J.
"American Plan" doesn't add up to much more than a social study about the oppression of a wide assortment of tyrannies.
Richard Greenberg’s drama The American Plan, set at a lakeside home in the Catskills during the summer of 1960, is an engrossing play with interesting spins on love and identity.
Director David Grindley extracts the laughs, while keeping the character-defining moments intact.

cn.t: Greenberg's elegant 1990 drama earns a worthy revival with incisive writing and compelling performances, particularly Ruehl's commanding turn as a domineering mother in this sharply acted exploration of fear and twisted love.

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.
